turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Popped Ned on the scales before you came in. Eighteen point four kilos, temp thirty six six, pulse ninety two. He was not keen on standing still.
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yeah he does that. Thanks. Sorry we're a bit late, the tram was a nightmare.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): I saw a blue tongue near the bins. It was huge. Can we get a biscuit from the jar after, the chocolate ones not the boring ones.
[SEG0004] person_4 (DOCTOR): Blue tongue, that's a good spot. Biscuit can wait till we're done. What's been going on with his skin?
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): These dry patches. Really itchy. Behind both knees and in the elbow creases. He scratches them raw, worse at night.
[SEG0006] person_4 (DOCTOR): How long have you noticed it?
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. I can't date it. Last winter, or the one before. I keep trying to remember and it just slides away.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ned, mate, does the itching stop you sleeping?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Banjo ate my vegemite sandwich. He sleeps on my bed and he burps. The sandwich was triangle cut.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ha, vegemite thief. We'll leave that. Mum, the nights?
[SEG0011] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most nights, yeah. Scratching in his sleep, then he's cranky as anything in the morning. School mornings are a write-off.
[SEG0012] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me look. Dry thickened patches in both elbow creases and behind both knees, and some scratch marks. Skin everywhere else looks fine. Nothing's weeping.

[SEG0013] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We've been putting stuff on from the chemist. Err, a white cream in a big tub, morning and night, for the dryness. And a little tube, pink writing, white cap, I dab that on the rough bits when he goes at them. I don't know what either of them's called, and sometimes I forget the tube for days.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right. Any fevers with this?
[SEG0015] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. He's been himself, temperature-wise.
[SEG0016] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any tummy troubles, vomiting, loose poos?
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, nothing like that. Eats like a horse, actually. Well, except broccoli, that's a whole saga.
[SEG0018] person_4 (DOCTOR): And any cough, or noisy breathing?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm. He had a sniffle, I don't know, maybe a little cough at bedtime a while back, but not really a cough now. Hard to say. Sorry, that's a muddle.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay, we'll not chase that. Any asthma or eczema in the family?
[SEG0021] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad's got asthma. Had it for years, puffer lives in his pocket. No eczema that I know of, just the asthma.
[SEG0022] person_3 (PATIENT): Dad's puffer is blue. I blew it once and I coughed and mum said don't. Can we go to the park with the big slide.

[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Park later, mate. Look, this is eczema to my eye, the atopic kind. The dry patches in the creases plus dad's asthma make me think that. I can't prove it today, but that's the working read.
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I knew it. He's only five, I don't want him on anything strong. His dad reckoned it was just the heater drying the air.

[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Put that little tube away and don't use it, we don't know if it's a steroid. I'll prescribe hydrocortisone one percent ointment, thin smear on the rough patches only, twice a day for seven days, then stop.
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The hydrocortazone? Twice a day, then stop. Yep, the little tube goes in the bin. I was slapping it on all over, which is probably wrong.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): Keep the white tub if it's just a plain moisturiser. Thick layer all over, morning and night, and again straight after a short lukewarm bath. Pat him dry, don't rub.
[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Baths every night? He hates them. He'll negotiate for forty minutes about the bubbles.

[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): Not every night if it's a battle. A few times a week is plenty, quick ones. I'll see you back in a fortnight. If it starts weeping or he gets hot and unwell, come back sooner, don't wait.
[SEG0030] person_3 (PATIENT): The slide is yellow. Banjo can't come because he eats the ducks. I want the chocolate biscuit.
[SEG0031] person_1 (NURSE): I'll book that fortnight with reception and send the script through. Chemist downstairs can fill the ointment if you want.
[SEG0032] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No worries. I think we're right. Thanks for not rushing us.

spec.situation: Mother brings a child with itchy dry patches behind the knees and elbows, worse at night, scratching; creams named by colour; father has asthma; doctor adjusts steroid cream and moisturiser advice.

traps.happens: The doctor asks only two to four review-of-systems questions (for example fever, weight, cough). Several other body systems are never asked about. One of the asked questions gets a vague or mixed answer.
traps.label_rule: negative_findings / review_of_systems ONLY for items the doctor actually asked AND the patient answered, evidence = that question and answer. Never add review-of-systems entries for systems nobody asked about, and never cite an unrelated turn (for example a turn about tiredness) for a system review.

features: patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
vague_dates: the patient cannot date things ('since Diwali or after', 'last winter, or the one before'); no invented date; a date_uncertain item.
